deep.reconstruction:
There are no derivations, formulas or computations on this page. It is a sequence of methodological and historical aphorisms, apparently notes for a lecture or essay on the nature of mathematics. It continues the previous page, whose last fragment ends mid-word, and the next page.

(a) Continuation of a programme, roughly: '...the ideas that can be named by catchwords [Schlag-/Stichworte] should be picked out and put together.' Examples given: the principle of uniqueness (Eindeutigkeit), the principle of necessary and sufficient conditions, and the group concept. The next page resumes this theme ('Aus allen mathematischen Wissensgebieten die wichtigsten und mit einem Schlag-[worte zu bezeichnenden Ideen]').

(b) A warning against seeing mathematical matters as in a distorting mirror ('Fixirspiegel', i.e. Vexier-/Vexirspiegel). In such a mirror the present and the modern appear excessively enlarged and the past strongly shrunk. This is a plea for historical fairness.

(c) Item '4.': The ancients also had the continuum, and were even close to grasping it, citing 'panta rhei' (Heraclitus) and the resting arrow (Zeno's arrow paradox). But only when the first attempt at a mathematical-axiomatic formulation succeeded did a deeper understanding arise.

Marginal addition, my reading: 'Even Gauss and d'Alembert did not know that behind the intuition of the continuum lies the Bolzano axiom. Only with the conquest of the continuum thus achieved, i.e. only then, came the incorporation of geometry, this hitherto richest province, into the realm of mathematics [arithmetic/analysis].'

In modern terms, 'Bolzano's axiom' is the least-upper-bound / Bolzano–Weierstrass completeness property of the reals. Bolzano proved the intermediate value theorem in 1817 using a supremum principle, and later this was formulated axiomatically. Hilbert himself added it as the Vollständigkeitsaxiom (completeness axiom) in the Grundlagen der Geometrie (2nd edition 1903, axiom already in the 1900 Zahlbegriff paper). The thesis is that geometry becomes part of arithmetized mathematics once the continuum is captured axiomatically, via coordinates over a complete ordered field.

(d) Start of the aphorism finished on the previous page: 'If someone without any prior education, unable to read and write, after hearing my lecture [brought the solution of the Riemann prime number problem]...' This dates the page as a fair copy belonging with the preceding page.
errors: Historical: attributing an 'axiom' to Bolzano is loose. Bolzano (1817) argued for the least-upper-bound property as a theorem, with a flawed proof since no construction of the reals was available. It was Dedekind, Cantor and Weierstrass, and Hilbert himself in 1900, who made completeness an axiom or construction. Hilbert's shorthand is defensible but anachronistic.

The claim that Gauss and d'Alembert 'did not know' the completeness principle is broadly fair. Gauss's 1799 proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra tacitly used continuity and intermediate-value properties without justification, so this is accurate as a characterization.

deep.surprise_reason: These are philosophical and methodological aphorisms consistent with Hilbert's known views: the completeness axiom, arithmetization of geometry, the role of the axiomatic method, and 'every problem is solvable' rhetoric. Hilbert's lecture notes on the nature of mathematics, e.g. 'Wissen und mathematisches Denken' and the 1919/20 lectures, contain similar remarks. The explicit naming of 'Bolzano's axiom' and the Heraclitus/Zeno reference are nice biographical details but not mathematically new.

checkable.asserts: Illustration of completeness: the bounded increasing sequence 1-1/n has limit (supremum) 1 in the reals.
Intermediate-value/Bolzano: x^3-2 changes sign on [1,2] and its root (cube root of 2, irrational) exists only in a complete field; difference is ~0.
